lines.note: Sangiuco is explained as three supreme ranks in Buddhism. The upright domain label visibly reads Bup., not the truncated OCR Bu.
Completes the reference to ranks discussed in Buddhist teaching. Buppò is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation, with the printed grave retained.
Sangiuin names a book described as a dictionary of written characters. The gloss begins vocabulario across the physical break.
Completes vocabulario deletras, specifying a character dictionary. The close printed deletras is retained rather than regularized to modern spacing.
Sango means after childbirth; the paired expression begins contrasting the periods after and before delivery. The final san- belongs to sanjen below.
Jen completes sanjen, before childbirth. The Portuguese explicitly gives the two periods in the same order as the Japanese pair.

runs.text: Sango. Tama tama. i, Meixuno na.

lines.note: This separate sango entry names a precious stone, rather than the postpartum period. The unusual printed Tama tama and Meixuno na are retained, not rewritten from the expected lexical identification.
Dra completes pedra: a precious stone bearing this name. The source gives a general precious-material gloss, without a more precise mineral description.
Sango is paraphrased as three acts or operations. The circumflex distinguishes this printed headword from the unaccented entries above.
Specifies operations of the eyes, ears, and tongue. This is the dictionary's own explanation, not an invitation to substitute a different doctrinal list.
The example calls for quieting these three activities and reciting this scripture. Docu- continues into ju; the repeated headword retains its circumflex.
Ju completes dokuju, scriptural recitation. The upright Taif. citation is followed by italic Lib. 20.; Aquie continues into aquietando without a securely visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: tando os olhos, ouuidos, & lingua. i, com

lines.note: Completes aquietando and repeats the eyes, ears, and tongue, then paraphrases the action as reading attentively. The scan supports ouuidos, not OCR ouxidos.
Concludes the translation: you will read this book with attention. Liuro is the historical u/v spelling for book, not OCR ſiuro.

runs.text: Sangocu. Mitçuno cuni. i, Tǒdo, Tengicu,

lines.note: Sangoku means three countries; the following names enumerate them. The small explanatory i, after cuni is present in the scan and was lost in the draft.
Wagacho completes the Japanese enumeration. The Portuguese names China, Siam, and Japan; its Sião is preserved even though Tengicu conventionally points to India. Ia- continues below.
Completes Iapão, Japan, as the last of the three kingdoms. This short continuation remains a separate physical body row.
Ise sangu is a pilgrimage to the deity named Tenxǒ daijin in the Portuguese gloss. The name's visible long-o caron replaces the OCR tilde.

runs.text: que he hum Cami de grande romaria que eſta no

lines.note: Describes this kami as the object of a major pilgrimage. Cami is a Japanese religious term within an otherwise Portuguese clause.
Locates the pilgrimage in the province called Ixe, Ise. The place name is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Sange is glossed through shame and repentance, then as confession or disclosure. Ma- continues into manifestar on the next row.
Completes manifestar and gives an example of confessing sins. The accent over Zaixǒ is a caron; Con- is entirely italic Portuguese, not a mixed-font Japanese fragment.
Completes confessar and explains revealing one's sins. The worn verb reads deſcobrir in the scan, rather than the OCR's deſcobrar.
This homographic sange means below the mountain, not confession. The Portuguese visibly has the historical double-vowel pee.
Sangueo denotes three teachings. The initial S, omitted by OCR, is visible; the printed gueô spelling is retained rather than normalized to a modern romanization.

runs.text: de tres meſtres, ou philoſophos antiguos. ſ.

lines.note: The teachings are attributed to three ancient masters or philosophers. The abbreviation at the end introduces their names below.
Names Shaka, Laozi, and Confucius as the three teachers. The first name reads Xaca, not Xica; these are names completing a Portuguese enumeration.

runs.text: Paoſinhos, ou tentos das ſortes, ou cõtas.

lines.note: Sangi are small rods or counters used for lots or calculations. The printed nasal abbreviation in cõtas is retained unexpanded.
Directs the reader to San for related information about the counting or divination rods. San is a Japanese cross-reference within Portuguese apparatus.
Sangyo is the form or appearance of a mountain, supported by Yamano catachi. OCR Nanano and the spurious italic letter inside the headword are corrected from the scan.
Te completes monte. The upright S. marks written usage; the additional OCR letters are show-through, not further text.

runs.text: Tres eſquadrões de gente militar que

lines.note: Sangun denotes three military divisions. The following rows specify the strength of each division rather than defining another entry.

runs.text: tem cada hum dous mil, & quinhentos ſol-

lines.note: States that each of the three divisions contains two thousand five hundred soldiers. Sol- continues into soldados below.
Completes soldados and the numerical explanation of the military divisions. Nothing is added to the printed troop count.
Sanze denotes three times or ages. Quaco and guẽzai name past and present; the tilde in guẽzai remains unexpanded.
Mirai completes the Japanese list with the future. The Portuguese repeats past, present, and future; preſente begins with the printed lowercase p.

runs.text: O entrar a tomar os põtos

lines.note: Sanzen, also given as sangaku, concerns receiving subjects for Zen meditation. The abbreviated põtos introduces the points themselves on the next line.

runs.text: da meditação dosIenxùs, ou os meſmos pontos.

lines.note: Completes the definition as the Zen practitioners' meditation topics, or those topics themselves. Ienxùs is the Japanese sect designation within Portuguese; pontos corrects OCR pantos.
This distinct sanjen means before childbirth, contrasting with sango earlier on the page. It is not part of the meditation entry.
Another sanjen is glossed by the printed Cacayaqi, u, corresponding to kagayaku, to shine. The source spelling is retained; the initial is S, not OCR B, and the final upright S. marks written usage.
The principal forms of sanzuru and the paraphrase chirasu introduce releasing or venting something. The Portuguese verb has f in Deſabafar, not the OCR long-s substitution.
Ki wo sanzuru is explained as unburdening the heart. This supplies the emotional sense of the preceding verb entry.
Ikon wo sanzuru is avenging a grievance. Mu- starts mune on the following row, introducing further objects of the same verb.
Mune, ikidowori, and uppun continue the expressions for venting resentment. The final i in iqidouori and italic Idẽ. replace incomplete and mixed-font OCR readings.
A separate sanzuru entry means to go or come. Ir is a Portuguese infinitive here, not OCR Vr or a Japanese fragment.
The example goko no sanjin begins describing an itinerant person. The Portuguese definition continues over the final two rows of the column.

runs.text: peßoa que anda por diuerſas partes, ſem ter lu-

lines.note: Describes a person wandering through different places without a fixed location. The scan supports peßoa, diuerſas, and ſem; lu- begins lugar.
Completes lugar and adds the absence of a settled dwelling. This is running body text above the bottom rule, not a catchword.
Sanjin is paraphrased as yamabito, a person of the wilderness or mountains. This is a separate entry from the itinerant-person example at the end of column 1.
Completes the definition as someone dwelling in the mountains. The final S. is an upright written-usage label, outside the italic gloss.
Sanjo means above or on the mountain. Yamano vye and the Portuguese gloss support the spatial sense; Encima remains printed as one word.
This sanjo denotes a mountain fortress. The Portuguese locative clause continues on the next short row.
Completes the mountain-fortress definition. The word belongs to the preceding entry, not an independent item.

runs.text: Ir a caſa de alguem, falando com reſ-

lines.note: Another sanjo means respectfully going to someone's house. The headword contains n, not OCR u; reſ- continues into respeito.
Completes respeito and marks the expression as written usage. The label S. is upright rather than part of the italic Portuguese word.
Shiro e mairu explains going to a fortress. This entry differs from the preceding respectful visit to a private house.
Sanjo is a place where a child is born. The unaccented final o is retained; na- begins the printed nacimento, continued below.

runs.text: cimento, ou lugar onde a molher pario.

lines.note: Completes nacimento and clarifies the place where a woman gave birth. Enlargement shows the full printed n, not an abbreviation tilde.

Introduces three objects regarded as the rulers' treasures. Iingui has consonantal initial I, matching the upright I of Iconuo on this page; the scan supports this reading over OCR ſingui. The supplied NINJAL entry also points to jingui, without controlling the diplomatic spelling.

runs.text: ſouro dos reis de Iapão. ſ.

lines.note: Completes tesouro and begins naming the three treasures. Reis and Iapão replace the garbled OCR; the abbreviation ſ. introduces the Japanese enumeration.
Xidocoro completes naixidocoro across the physical break. The following Latin instruction directs readers to the individual entries for these names.
Sanmai is a burial ground, paraphrased as hakadokoro and glossed as a churchyard or cemetery. The scan reads docoro, not OCR docoto.
Sanman describes scattering or spreading, here introducing the falling of many flowers or leaves. The paired Japanese verbs guide the following extended gloss.

runs.text: muitas flores, ou folhas de aruores muito baſtas,

lines.note: Continues the falling of many flowers or leaves from very dense trees. The historical aruores spelling and the physical line break are retained.

runs.text: & floridas. ¶ Item, Modo de ſe aleuantar

lines.note: Completes the description of flowering trees, then introduces another sense: the rising or spreading of a cloud of dust.

runs.text: grande poeira com correr de caualos, ou encõtro

lines.note: Describes much dust raised by running horses or a military encounter. The abbreviation in encõtro is preserved in the canonical text.
Completes the warfare example. The separate upright S. marks the entry as belonging to written usage.
Sanmichi denotes a three and an ace on dice. The Portuguese nos dados is two words, correcting the OCR join.
The phrase is equated with exposing one's shame. The scan's ſagaſu is retained rather than silently assimilated to ſaraſu in the explanatory Japanese phrase.
Completes ficar: becoming ashamed or disgraced in front of people. This establishes the public-humiliation sense of the Japanese expression.
Sanmon santo is explained as asking three times. The following row gives the corresponding three replies.
Mitabi kotayuru means answering three times. The Portuguese translates the pair as three questions and replies; re- continues into the source spelling repoſtas on the next row.

runs.text: poſtas. i, Tres exames que ſe fazem diante

lines.note: Completes the printed repoſtas, without inserting the additional s of modern respostas, and recasts the procedure as three examinations. The capital T in Tres corrects OCR Pres.

runs.text: do juiz antre o reo, & autor pera aueriguar

lines.note: Specifies examination before a judge between defendant and plaintiff to establish the facts. Historical antre, reo, and pera are preserved.
Completes the explanation with the lawsuit or claim under investigation. It is a short continuation of the judicial example.

runs.text: Portal, ou porta principal, que hà

lines.note: This sanmon is a main temple gate. The definition continues with the type of religious buildings and the upper storey.

runs.text: nas varelas dos Ienxùs com ſobrado em cima.

lines.note: Describes the principal gate of Zen temples with an upper floor. The Japanese sect name reads Ienxùs, not OCR Iencũs, and remains marked as an embedded term.
Sanmon no shuto refers here to the monks of the mountain named below. The Portuguese reads Bonzos, correcting the OCR vowel in Banzos.
Names Mount Hiei as the location of these monks. Fiyeno yama completes a Portuguese definition and is therefore an embedded Japanese name, not a fresh headword.
Sannai is explained as within the mountains, a wilderness or place among mountains. The Portuguese clause continues below.
Completes the locative definition as a place among the mountains. This is part of sannai, not a new headword.
Sannan is the third son. The short Portuguese gloss fixes the birth-order meaning.
Sanni denotes a three and a two on dice. This parallels the three-and-ace combination defined earlier.

runs.text: Terceira meſa que ſe poem nos

lines.note: San no zen is the third serving table or tray placed at a banquet. The Portuguese description continues below.
Completes the banquet setting of the third tray. The clear printed banquetes replaces the heavily garbled OCR paBaueres.
The example denotes a past time. Both occurrences visibly carry a tilde in Sãnuru, which is retained without expanding the nasal abbreviation.
Sanomi is an adverb glossed as so much or to that extent. Aduer. is italic grammatical apparatus, not part of the Japanese form.
Sanpai is worshipping or bowing three times. The entire Portuguese Tres vezes ado- is italic; the faint intervening marks are show-through, not a secure printed paragraph sign.
Completes adorar and gives sanpai suru, making three acts of reverence. The Portuguese Fa- begins Fazer across the next break.
Completes the translation as performing three adorations or reverences. These are repeated gestures, consistent with mitabi in the Japanese paraphrase.
This separate sanpai means going to pay one's respects or worship. The paraphrase mairi vogamu differs from the preceding threefold act.
The polite Japanese example promises to speak when making a respectful visit. The historical formula is retained without modernizing its spelling or inserting particles.

runs.text: Falarei quando for abeijar as mãos de V. M.

lines.note: Translates the promise as speaking when coming to kiss the addressee's hands. For and mãos correct the OCR's fer and midos; the source's joined abeijar is retained.

runs.text: Conſonancia, ou armonia que ſe faz

lines.note: Sanpyoshi is concord or harmony produced together. Conſonancia, not OCR Conſenancia, is the visible Portuguese noun.

runs.text: com tres couſas. ſ. Frauta, tabaquinho, &

lines.note: Names a flute and a small drum as the first two elements; the third continues on f436. Frauta is the chosen reading of the abraded instrument name, with its damaged first vowel remaining a nonblocking caveat.
